identification.description: An invasive lepidopteran pest, native to the Americas, first reported on maize in India in May 2018. It has since spread to over 90% of maize-growing areas across India's diverse agro-ecologies.
key_features: Larvae feed on maize leaves, whorl, stem, and cobs
Characteristic 'window-pane' feeding damage and ragged holes on young whorl leaves
Larvae bore into stems and cobs, causing structural damage
Frass (larval excreta) visible in the whorl

affected_crops: Also reported on sorghum and millets in India with varying economic damage
damage_symptoms: Window-pane feeding lesions on young leaves
Ragged, irregular holes in whorl leaves as larvae mature
Hollowed-out stems and damaged cobs in severe infestation
Visible larval frass in the whorl
monitoring: Regular field scouting of the whorl for egg masses, young larvae, and characteristic window-pane damage, especially in the first 30-40 days after crop emergence
Pheromone traps for adult moth monitoring (specific trap density/threshold NOT VERIFIED in this batch)

cultural: NOT VERIFIED - pending direct-source confirmation beyond the secondary report used for chemical guidance below.
biological: Bracon hebetor (a larval parasitoid) has been studied for efficacy against S. frugiperda in India per Sree Latha et al. 2019 (Indian Journal of Entomology) - cited as a research finding, NOT yet confirmed as an operational field recommendation in this batch.

guidance.dose: 70-80 ml in 200 litres of water per acre, sprayed to thoroughly cover upper and lower leaf surfaces
guidance.source_note: Reported as an ICAR-IARI (Indian Agricultural Research Institute) recommendation via a secondary news report (global-agriculture.com, July 2025). This dose is also consistent with the 0.4 ml/L rate (~80 ml/200L) studied at ICAR-Indian Institute of Maize Research, Hyderabad (Plant Science Today, 2025).

official_chemical_guidance.important_note: The Chlorantraniliprole dose above is corroborated by two independent sources (a secondary report of an IARI recommendation, and a peer-reviewed field study from ICAR-IIMR), but the PRIMARY IARI/ICAR advisory document itself was not directly located and fetched in this batch. Before farmer-facing deployment, locate and cite the primary ICAR/IARI or state agricultural university advisory directly, and confirm current CIB&RC registration status for this product on maize.

expert_consultation_required_when: Infestation is detected in more than a small percentage of the whorl-stage plants
You need confirmation of the primary source document before large-scale spraying
You are unsure whether whorl damage is fall armyworm vs. another stem borer/caterpillar pest

sources.source_name: Global Agriculture (secondary report of IARI recommendation)
sources.source_title: Fall Armyworm Threatens Maize Crops in India: IARI Recommends Immediate Control Measures
Evaluation of phenology-based insecticide strategies for fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda) management in maize in India

data_quality.notes: Biology, spread, and one corroborated chemical dose are sourced. IP102 class_id/canonical_name mapping, cultural/mechanical IPM steps, and the primary ICAR/IARI advisory document are still pending. Do not treat as fully verified until the primary source is located.

identification.description: A phloem-sucking insect (Nilaparvata lugens) that causes 'hopperburn' in rice. Nymphs hatch creamy-white then turn dark brown, and adults are brownish-black. Severe infestations produce dry, yellow-brown patches (hopperburn) and lodging.
symptoms: Rice plants show yellowing and drying of lower leaves (hopperburn) under heavy infestation
White to dark-brown nymphs and brown adults feeding on leaf sheaths and tiller bases
Honeydew and sooty mold often appear on undersides of leaves

risk_factors: Warm, humid weather and excessive nitrogen favor BPH outbreaks
Stagnant water and continuous rice cropping increase pest buildup
High winds can carry migrant hoppers from nearby fields

immediate_non_chemical_actions: Monitor rice fields from tillering to flowering for first hopper sighting (1 hopper/tiller = ETL)
Set up yellow water-pan or light traps to detect migratory adults
cultural_management: Use wider spacing (~30 cm row gaps) and alternate wet/dry irrigation
mechanical_or_physical_management: Drain the paddy water briefly before spraying to expose insects
biological_management: Spray neem oil (3%) or azadirachtin (0.03%) as botanical control
Preserve natural enemies (spiders) by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides

guidance.caution_flag: Carbosulfan has restricted/withdrawn registration status in several contexts in India - do NOT present this as currently approved without an independent CIB&RC check specifically for this active ingredient before any field use.

official_chemical_guidance.important_note: Dosages are as published on the TNAU Agritech Portal (rice pest management). Efficacy depends on application timing and water management. Verify current CIB&RC registration status before use - note Carbosulfan specifically has restricted status in several contexts and needs independent confirmation.

prevention: Rotate rice with non-host crops (legumes, oilseeds) to reduce BPH carryover
Deep plow stubble after harvest to reduce overwintering inoculum

mild: Examine hopper counts weekly; if under 1 per tiller, continue observation.
moderate: Apply a protectant insecticide (e.g. Acetamiprid or Fipronil) when hoppers reach threshold.
high: For severe hopperburn, apply insecticide promptly and consult local KVK for emergency measures.

records.farmer_warning: Brown planthopper can rapidly kill rice stands via 'hopperburn' if unmanaged, especially around the flowering stage.
expert_consultation_required_when: Hopperburn symptoms appear across more than half the field before flowering
Uncertainty whether damage is caused by BPH or another planthopper species
Need advice on pesticide resistance or restricted-status actives like Carbosulfan

india_context.region_notes: Guidance is based on TNAU (Tamil Nadu) recommendations. Check with your State Agricultural University for regional BPH management advice.

sources.source_title: Crop Protection - Paddy - Brown Plant Hopper (Nilaparvata lugens)

data_quality.notes: Identification and control measures verified from TNAU rice pest guide. One listed active ingredient (Carbosulfan) is flagged for independent registration-status confirmation before use.

identification.description: A caterpillar pest whose larvae fold rice leaves lengthwise and scrape out the green tissue. Young folded leaves turn white and dry; heavy infestations give the field a scorched look. Adults are small yellowish-brown moths with dark wavy lines.
symptoms: Longitudinally rolled (folded) leaves with white patches inside
Greenish, translucent larvae within rolled leaves
Severely affected fields appear yellow or burned due to dead leaf tissue

risk_factors: Dense canopy or excessive nitrogen increases outbreak risk
Continuous flooding may favor leaf folder buildup

immediate_non_chemical_actions: Release egg parasitoids (Trichogramma chilonis) at 2 cc/acre, three times (30, 37, 44 days after sowing)
Apply NSKE 5% or Azadirachtin 0.03% (400 ml/acre) when infestation begins
mechanical_or_physical_management: Promptly remove and destroy heavily rolled leaves during early stages
biological_management: Trichogramma chilonis egg parasitoid releases (see immediate actions)

guidance.caution_flag: Carbosulfan has restricted/withdrawn registration status in several contexts in India - verify current CIB&RC status independently.

official_chemical_guidance.important_note: Rates as given by TNAU Agritech Portal for rice leaf folder. Sprays should begin at early leaf-rolling. Verify product registration under the Insecticides Act before use.

prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant rice varieties if available
Follow recommended sowing dates to avoid peak pest migrations

mild: Monitor weekly; start NSKE/Azadirachtin sprays if rolling begins.
moderate: Apply a recommended insecticide (e.g. Chlorantraniliprole or Thiamethoxam) per TNAU schedule.
high: If over 10% of plants show rolling, apply chemical controls promptly and consult KVK.

records.farmer_warning: Leaf roller damage can significantly reduce yield if it progresses into the flowering (panicle) stage.
expert_consultation_required_when: Rolling is widespread beyond threshold levels
Unclear if damage is leaf roller or another borer/pest

india_context.region_notes: Based on the TNAU rice pest bulletin. Verify local compatibility, e.g. avoid broad-spectrum sprays that harm beneficial insects.

sources.source_title: Crop Protection - Paddy - Leaf Folder / Leaf Roller (Cnaphalocrocis medinalis)

data_quality.notes: Spray rates and IPM measures taken from the TNAU paddy pest guide. One active ingredient (Carbosulfan) flagged for registration-status confirmation.

identification.description: Small, soft-bodied, sap-sucking insects. Colonies of greenish or yellowish aphids cluster on tender shoots and leaf undersides, excreting honeydew that leads to sooty mold. Common species include Aphis gossypii on okra/cotton and A. craccivora on legumes.
symptoms: Leaf curling, puckering, and yellowing on young shoots
Stunted growth and shriveling of tender foliage
Sticky honeydew and black sooty mold on leaves
Clusters of tiny pear-shaped insects on shoot tips

risk_factors: Warm, dry conditions accelerate aphid population growth
Ants tending colonies can worsen infestations

immediate_non_chemical_actions: Remove severely infested leaves or plants
Use a strong jet of water to dislodge aphids early in the day
cultural_management: Practice clean cultivation: destroy weeds that serve as aphid reservoirs
mechanical_or_physical_management: Yellow sticky traps to monitor and reduce flights
Control ant nests near fields (ants farm aphid colonies)
biological_management: Neem formulations or Lecanicillium lecanii - ICAR-IGFRI found L. lecanii (2 g/L) and neem (3000 ppm) effective on cowpea aphid

guidance.dose: 400 ml/acre (25% EC) - for wheat, threshold 10-15 aphids/tiller
guidance.caution_flag: Quinalphos is a WHO Class Ib organophosphate - verify current registration status before recommending.

official_chemical_guidance.important_note: Chemical guidance is crop-specific (see dose notes) and drawn from TNAU (okra) and an ICAR-IIWBR advisory (wheat) reported via secondary news coverage, not the primary ICAR document. Always match the guidance to the actual host crop and verify current registration before use.

prevention: Maintain balanced crop nutrition to avoid excessive tender growth attractive to aphids

mild: Monitor for ant trails or small colonies; treat only if expanding.
moderate: Begin chemical control with a crop-appropriate, labelled insecticide.
high: For heavy infestation, rotate insecticide chemistry and seek local advisory - some aphids transmit viral diseases requiring integrated management.

records.farmer_warning: Aphids can rapidly multiply and also spread viral diseases (e.g. YVMV in okra, BYDV in wheat) - early control matters more than the direct feeding damage alone.
expert_consultation_required_when: Widespread stunting or unexplained honeydew is present
You need to confirm which host crop's guidance applies

india_context.region_notes: This is a broad pest category covering multiple aphid species across different host crops (see crop_pest_mapping.json for okra, wheat, cowpea entries). The model detects 'aphids' generically without identifying species or host crop from the image alone - the app should ask the farmer to confirm their crop before showing crop-specific dosage.

Eco-Friendly Aphid Management in Fodder Cowpea

data_quality.notes: Multi-crop pest; dosage guidance is crop-specific and must be matched to farmer's actual crop, not applied generically. One source (ICAR wheat advisory) is secondary, not primary.
